title: No Triangulation Without Representation: Generalization in Topological Deep Learning
claim: The same object can be encoded in several distinct representations that preserve different amounts of structural information.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, matching colors link the same cells across panels
description: Three side-by-side panels show the same 2-sphere, which is a triangulation with 4 triangles, in three encodings. Panel (a) is a simplicial complex. It is a flattened triangulated shape with four filled triangles σ1 to σ4 in yellow, blue, green and orange. Vertices v1 to v4 and edges e1 to e6 are labeled, and dotted arrows show which boundary edges and vertices are identified. Panel (b) is a layered Hasse diagram. The top row holds the four colored triangle nodes, the middle row holds six grey edge nodes, and the bottom row holds four grey vertex nodes. Thin lines join each cell to its faces. Panel (c) is the dual graph, which is K4. The four colored triangle nodes are connected by edges labeled e1 to e6, with e1 dashed. The eye goes first to the colored triangle in (a), then follows the matching colors across the panels. Captions sit under each panel.
caption: Three representations of $S^2$, the $2$-sphere. The simplicial complex and Hasse diagram contain the same information, while the dual graph only represents maximal simplex connectivity.
abstract: Despite an ever-increasing interest in topological deep learning models that target higher-order datasets, there is no consensus on how to evaluate such models. This is exacerbated by the fact that topological objects permit operations, such as structural refinements, that are not appropriate for graph data. In this work, we extend MANTRA, a benchmark dataset containing manifold triangulations, to a larger class of manifolds with more diverse homeomorphism types. We show that, contrary to prior claims, graph neural networks can saturate the benchmark, while higher-order message passing methods lag behind. However, we find that this is contingent on the right representation and feature assignment, emphasizing their importance in baseline models. Hence, we present a novel evaluation protocol based on representational diversity and triangulation refinement. Even when including refinement-like changes in the training data, existing models fail to generalize beyond the combinatorial structure of the data. This points towards a research gap in developing models that understand topological structure independent of scale. Our work thus provides the necessary scaffolding to evaluate future models and enable the development of topology-aware inductive biases.
